Securely
se-cure'ly
adv. (without fear or apprehension; in the older English, carelessly, without watchfulness)
Latin securus, from se-, without, and cura, care — literally without care. The old English sense is therefore not safe but unworried, which may be a virtue or a fatal negligence.

Biblical Definition

The Latin root matters: securus is without care, and the Authorized Version uses the adverb for people who are not looking over their shoulders — once innocently, once tragically. Solomon: “Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee” (Pro 3:29). The neighbour's trust is itself the argument. He lives beside you without a guard because he assumes you are not plotting, and to exploit that assumption is the aggravation of the offence — the next verse adds, “Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm” (Pro 3:30). Micah describes the same trust being robbed, and by the covenant people: “Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war” (Mic 2:8). The victims are travellers who were not expecting trouble, and the robbers are God's own people. Judges shows the other face of the word, where security is simple negligence: Laish dwelt careless and secure, with no magistrate in the land, and was destroyed (Jdg 18:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines securely as without fear or apprehension; carelessly; in an unguarded state; and notes that the Latin securus is without care.

expand to see more

SECU'RELY, adv.

1. Without fear or apprehension; without care or anxiety.

His neighbor dwelleth securely by him. Prov. 3.

2. Carelessly; in an unguarded state.

SECU'RE, a. [L. securus; se, without, and cura, care.] Free from danger; safe; and also, careless; wanting caution.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 3:29 — "Devise not evil against thy neighbour, seeing he dwelleth securely by thee."

Micah 2:8 — "Even of late my people is risen up as an enemy: ye pull off the robe with the garment from them that pass by securely as men averse from war."

Proverbs 3:30 — "Strive not with a man without cause, if he have done thee no harm."

Judges 18:7 — "Then the five men departed, and came to Laish, and saw the people that were therein, how they dwelt careless, after the manner of the Zidonians, quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land, that might put them to shame in any thing; and they were far from the Zidonians, and had no business with any man."

Modern Corruption

Trust is now treated as a weakness that invites exploitation, so that the betrayal of it becomes the victim's fault.

expand to see more

Proverbs 3:29 grounds a prohibition in the neighbour's defencelessness: do not devise evil against him seeing he dwelleth securely by thee. The modern instinct runs the other way — a man who did not lock the door, who trusted the wrong person, who failed to protect himself, is held partly responsible for what was done to him. Scripture puts the whole weight on the one who exploited the trust, and treats the trust itself as something owed protection rather than punished. That principle runs through the law's protection of the widow, the stranger, and the fatherless, and it is why the abuse of a trusted office is treated in Scripture as an aggravation, never a mitigation.

Micah 2:8 supplies the sharpest form of the charge, and the church should not read past it: the robbers are my people, stripping travellers who were averse from war — peaceable men who never expected it. Wolves inside the fold is not a modern discovery. And Judges 18:7 keeps the balance by showing the other sense of the word: Laish was quiet and secure with no magistrate in the land, and that carelessness was ruin. The dictionary holds both — trust is a good that the trustworthy must guard, and the absence of any lawful authority is not peace but an invitation.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew betach (H983), securely, in confidence; batach (H982), to trust; shoqet (H8252), quiet, undisturbed; Latin securus, without care.

expand to see more

Hebrew lavetach (H983) — in confidence, securely; Proverbs 3:29, the neighbour living without a guard.

Hebrew batach (H982) — to trust, to lean upon; the root, and the standard word for trusting in the LORD.

Hebrew shuve milchamah — turned back from war, averse from war; Micah 2:8, the peaceable travellers robbed.

Hebrew shoqet uvoteach (H8252, H982) — quiet and secure; Judges 18:7, of Laish before its destruction.

Latin se- and cura — without care; Webster's root, which is why security can mean safety or negligence.

Usage

"“Seeing he dwelleth securely by thee” — his trust is the reason, not the excuse."

"“Them that pass by securely as men averse from war” — and the robbers are my people."

"“Quiet and secure; and there was no magistrate in the land” — the other sense, and it was ruin."
